points.title: System implementation and the implementation plan
points.must: Both definitions: implementation = installing, transferring data, training, changing over; the plan = how, when and by whom, with tasks, order, dates, responsible people, resources and contingency.
points.model: System implementation — the stage in which the new system is installed, the data is transferred, users are trained and the organisation changes over from the old system. System implementation plan — a document that describes how, when and by whom the new system will be installed and put into use: every task, its order, dates, responsible people, resources and what to do if something goes wrong.

points.title: Why the plan is important
points.must: At least six reasons, each explained: no task forgotten, correct order (dependencies), on time (dates, milestones), roles, budget/resources, less risk and disruption, success can be checked.
points.model: 1) No task is forgotten (accounts, data, training). 2) Tasks are in the correct order — dependencies. 3) Goes live on time — dates and milestones let managers see delays early. 4) A responsible person for every task. 5) Budget and resources controlled (staff time, trainers, equipment). 6) Reduces risk (backup, verification, testing, contingency) and disruption (work at quiet times). 7) Success can be reviewed against the plan.

points.title: What goes wrong without a plan (clinic example)
points.must: Problems without a plan and the clinic example: training after go-live, appointments not entered, no fallback vs. backed up, checked, trained before go-live, paper book kept as contingency.
points.model: Without a plan: staff not trained, data lost or wrong, hardware late, no backup, over budget. Clinic: without a plan receptionists are trained after go-live and next month's appointments are missing. With a plan: appointments backed up, entered and checked the week before, training Thu–Fri, go-live Monday 08:00, paper book kept two weeks as contingency.

points.title: The method is only one element
points.must: Direct / parallel / pilot / phased is one element; how the method shapes the plan (direct: everything ready by one date; parallel: work in both systems; pilot/phased: repeat for each part).
points.model: The implementation method (direct, parallel, pilot, phased) is only ONE element of the plan. Direct — everything finished before one date, contingency critical. Parallel — period of working in both systems, extra staff time, date to compare and switch off. Pilot/phased — installation and training repeated for each department/part.

points.title: Elements of the plan
points.must: The twelve elements: method, schedule, hardware installation, software installation and accounts, data conversion, training, testing, responsibilities, resources and budget, risks and contingency, documentation and support, review.
points.model: Method · schedule/timetable with milestones · hardware installation · software installation, user accounts and access rights · data conversion · staff training (who, method, timing) · testing before go-live · responsibilities · resources and budget · risks and contingency plan · documentation and support · review/evaluation.

points.title: Installation, accounts and acceptance testing
points.must: Hardware first; software installation includes accounts with access rights; definition of acceptance testing; documentation, support and review after go-live.
points.model: Hardware installed early (delivery, cabling, checks). Software: install application and database, configure, create user accounts with access rights (receptionist books, only the doctor reads medical notes). Acceptance testing — testing by the client and users with realistic data to confirm the system meets the requirements before go-live. After go-live: user guide, technical documentation, help desk, review against the requirements.

points.title: Data conversion
points.must: Definition; back up first, then transfer, then verify, then go live.
points.model: Data conversion (migration) — transferring the existing data from the old system (paper or old files) into the new system in the format it needs, and checking it was transferred completely and correctly. Order: full backup of old data → transfer → verify → go live.

points.title: Conversion methods and checks
points.must: Manual entry, import/export, conversion program — when used, one advantage and disadvantage each; verification by double entry, record counts, totals, samples.
points.model: Manual entry from paper — no special software, but slow and typing errors → verify by double entry / visual check. Import/export (CSV, SQL scripts) — fast for thousands of records, but formats may not match → compare record counts and totals, sample checks. Conversion program — automatic, but must be written and tested → test on a copy first.

points.title: Why training matters and training methods
points.must: Why training is a separate element; the six methods with an advantage and disadvantage; choosing a method to fit the staff.
points.model: Untrained staff make errors, work slowly, return to old ways. Methods: classroom/group (questions answered, many at once / away from work); one-to-one (fits the learner / expensive); online videos (any time, own pace / no immediate help); manuals/quick guides (always available / not read); train the trainer (cheaper / depends on key users); practice mode (hands-on, no risk / setup time). Often combined.

points.title: Who is trained and when
points.must: Users, managers, technical staff; after the software is installed and just before go-live, refresher after, in shifts.
points.model: Who: users (everyday tasks), managers (reports, settings), technical staff (backups, accounts, faults). When: after the software is installed and just before go-live so staff remember; refresher help after go-live; in groups or shifts so work continues.

points.title: Ordering tasks and estimating time
points.must: Work backwards from go-live to find dependencies; estimate durations (calculation example); parallel tasks; definition of critical path.
points.model: Start from go-live and work backwards: go-live needs data, training, testing; training needs software; software needs hardware; conversion needs the database and a backup. Durations: 2 400 records ÷ 100 per hour = 24 h of work → 2 assistants × 4 h/day ≈ 3 days. Independent tasks run at the same time. Critical path — the longest chain of dependent tasks; a delay on it delays go-live.

points.title: Dependency, milestone, contingency plan
points.must: All three definitions with an example each.
points.model: Dependency — a task that cannot start until another has finished (training depends on the software being installed). Milestone — an important point marking the end of a stage, with a date but no duration (go-live 24.11). Contingency plan — what to do if something goes wrong (restore from backup, return to the old system, manual procedure).

points.title: Steps to make a plan
points.must: The eight steps in order: method, tasks, order/dependencies, durations/dates/milestones, responsible person, resources/budget, risks/contingency, table and Gantt chart.
points.model: 1) Choose and justify the method. 2) List all tasks. 3) Order them, note dependencies. 4) Estimate durations, set dates and milestones. 5) Assign a responsible person. 6) List resources and budget. 7) Identify risks, write a contingency plan. 8) Show as a table and a Gantt chart.

points.title: Example plan table and Gantt chart
points.must: Columns of the plan table (No., task, start, end, responsible, depends on) with library tasks; definition of a Gantt chart; table vs Gantt; reading durations and overlaps.
points.model: Plan table columns: No. | Task | Start | End | Responsible | Depends on (e.g. 4 Enter 2 400 book records, 08.11–20.11, librarian + 2 assistants, depends on 3). Gantt chart — bar chart of the schedule: a row per task, time left to right, bar length = duration, overlaps = tasks at the same time, diamonds = milestones. Table shows who/dependencies; Gantt shows the timeline and progress. Task 4 lasts 13 days.

points.title: Contingency risks and common mistakes
points.must: At least three risks with actions; the common mistakes in a plan.
points.model: Risks → actions: new system crashes → continue on paper, developer fixes; data entry late → more assistants; scanners late → type barcodes; data lost → restore from backup. Mistakes: training after go-live, conversion before installation or without backup, tasks with no dates or responsible person, no acceptance testing, no contingency, old system stopped before the new one is checked.
